sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification (Languages of the New Guinea Region). Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18323007. Sec. 4.7 'Southwest Tanimbar', pp. 240-248; also p. 444.
sources.note: Historical phonology only. Sec. 4.7 gives Makatian/Seluwasan/Selaru sound correspondences (*p > zero, *l > dʒ/d, *R reflexes) from Conner 2012 wordlists and Edwards fieldnotes; nothing on Seluwasan stress (grep of the LaTeX sources and full PDF text: no 'stress'/'accent' in the Southwest Tanimbar section). p. 444 states stress for relatives only: 'In Fordata, stress is penultimate. In Yamdena stress is normally penultimate, but can shift to the ultimate syllable with the addition of plural -ar. In Kei stress is ultimate.'

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen (recorder). 2025. Seluwasan wordlist 1 (item SWS001; 505-item UBB wordlist, handwritten IPA, 12 pp. scan; Wermatang speakers D. Kore, Y. Kore, P. Sainyakit, Y. Kelmanutu, D. Samangun; recorded 26 Apr 2025). In: Emplawas and languages of the Babar islands, ELAR deposit 0741-IPF0417. London: ELAR. hdl:2196/0cmml8zn-hg3u-3y7r-v04j-5vw7apoh6jv1 (open access).
sources.note: No prose statement. Primary data only: most transcribed forms carry an IPA primary-stress mark (ˈ). On the pages I read (pp. 1, 2, 4, 5) the mark sits on the penultimate syllable of consonant-final and CV-final forms (e.g. ˈmanuk 'bird', ˈnamuk 'mosquito', ˈmɛtum 'black', ˈsɔrun 'horn', ˈsasin 'one', ˈnarun 'long', ˈduran 'rotten', ˈʔawɛ 'tree', ˈdʒabɛ 'banana', kalˈkalɛ 'spider', laˈbrayɛ 'oyster', mɔsˈmɔsɛ), while forms written with an optional parenthesised final (ɛ) keep the mark on the penult of the ɛ-less base, i.e. surface antepenult (ʔaˈtaf(ɛ) 'leaf', ˈmadus(ɛ) 'betel', ˈdʒɛtum(ɛ) 'su…

sources.citation: Hughes, Jock. 1987. The languages of Kei, Tanimbar and Aru: Lexicostatistic classification. In Soenjono Dardjowidjojo (ed.), Miscellaneous studies of Indonesian and other languages in Indonesia, part 9 (NUSA 27), 71-111. Jakarta: Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya. Sec. 2.1.2.6 'Seluwasan', p. 89.
sources.note: Silent. The Seluwasan section (p. 89) gives location (Wermatang, Batu Putih, Marantutul + divergent Makatian dialect, c. 2,100 speakers), lexical similarity (Wermatang-Makatian 86%) and intelligibility anecdotes; no phonology. scanned of all 41 pages finds no 'stress'/'accent' anywhere; stress marks appear only in a table of Yamdena dialect forms (p. 104). Seluwasan wordlists themselves are not printed.
